> A persistence-of-vision (POV) display: a spinning arm with 16 APA102 RGB LEDs driven by an ESP32. A Hall sensor and a magnet detect each rotation, so the ESP32 can draw an image in the air. Powered by a removable LiPo battery on the rotor, spun by a small brushed DC motor.Onshape link: https://cad.onshape.com/documents/4df1f19cbef029885b42195c/w/202e8609e3d3d323b0620ab0/e/cf2daba3494b5e3bf764868f

### 2026-10-29: ## Week 4, Entry 1: research, design decisions and schematic

**4h**

## Week 4, Entry 1: research, design decisions and schematic

**Time:** 1.5 h of research and design decisions, 0.75 h writing the README, 0.5 h making the idea reel (all outside the timelapse), plus the timelapse of drawing the schematic in KiCad.
### Research and design decisions (1.5 h)

I am building SpinPOV, a persistence-of-vision display: a thin arm with 16 RGB LEDs spins very fast, and an ESP32 changes the LEDs many times per turn, so the eye sees a round image in the air.

I started with research and design decisions:

- **Motor:** I will use a simple brushed DC motor that I already have to spin the display.
- **Power:** I was deciding between a battery on the arm and power through slip rings. I decided on a battery, because I saw that many similar projects use one, and slip rings add parts and complexity. The battery also acts as a counterweight for the LED strip. It will be a removable 1S LiPo that I charge outside the rotor, so there is no charger on the arm.
- **LEDs:** I decided on RGB LEDs, so the display can show colour. I chose APA102, because they have a separate clock line and stay stable at high speed.
- **Controller:** ESP32 DevKit (30-pin), because I already have it. I considered an Arduino Nano, but it only has 2 KB of RAM, which is not enough for a colour image.
- **Sync:** an A3144 Hall sensor on the arm and a magnet on the base. Each pulse means a new revolution, so the ESP32 can measure the speed and divide each turn into columns. That is why the motor does not need exact speed control.
- **No custom PCB:** the parts will be wired onto a 3D-printed arm, but I still drew a full schematic.

### Schematic (timelapse)

![Zrzut ekranu 2026-10-28 182612](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/3cd3501542afd51db10e48e7fa91d80ad61b457f2a656f2af31eae735cff9635.png)

The timelapse shows me drawing the schematic in KiCad: ESP32, APA102 strip on SPI (GPIO23 data, GPIO18 clock), Hall sensor on GPIO27, battery with a switch, a MT3608 boost module for 5 V, capacitors, and the motor as a separate stationary block.

In the places where nothing changes on the screen, I was checking datasheets and information about the components I used.

### What I simplified

My first version had a charger module on the rotor and a pull-up resistor for the Hall sensor. Because everything spins, I removed all of it. The Hall sensor uses the ESP32's internal pull-up, the battery is charged outside.

### What went wrong

The KiCad ERC reported "power output connected to power output". The 3.3 V pin of the ESP32 symbol is already a power output, so my `PWR_FLAG` on it was a mistake. I removed it and the check passes.

### 2026-10-31: ## Week 4, Entry 2: CAD in Onshape, wall mount and balancing

**4.17h**

## Week 4, Entry 2: CAD in Onshape, wall mount and balancing

In this session I designed the whole mechanical part of SpinPOV in Onshape. The motor model, a wall bracket, the spinning arm with places for all electronics, and the mounting of the Hall sensor and magnet. I also solved a few problems I found on the way, and did some research on the parts.

### 1. Measuring the motor and modelling it
I measured my brushed DC motor. The shaft is 3 mm, the free part of the shaft is about 13 mm, the body is about 27 mm in diameter, and there are two 2 mm mounting holes on the shaft side, opposite each other. I modelled the motor in Onshape with the body, the shaft, the collar around the shaft, the mounting holes and the pins at the back, so that all other parts can be designed around real dimensions.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/8a19805d9ff0aafec85b510242b3721fd55dc2f5bb56a81a8ac4f04f7c610e0c.png)

### 2. Wall mount instead of a stand

I decided to screw the display to the side of my wardrobe, so I do not need any stand. The shaft is horizontal, the arm spins parallel to the wall, and the picture is visible from the room. In the CAD model the Z axis simply points from the wall to the room.

### 3. The bracket

The bracket is one printed part:

-  **front plate** (50 x 50 x 4 mm) with a hole for the shaft and , holes for the motor screws and recess for the magnet,
-  **back plate** (70 x 50 x 4 mm) with two 4.5 mm holes for wood screws into the wardrobe,
- **two side walls**(50x40x3 mm) connecting them, so the motor sits inside, between the plates.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/fd75f50f30891a12922fb63609d69dd43740e0bd0bf4802e69f835001e462be5.png)

### 4. The spinning arm

The arm is 240 x 38 x 4 mm and is one part with a hub that sits on the 3 mm shaft. I added these features:

-  **pocket for the LED strip** on the top (111 mm long, for 16 LEDs of a 144 LED/m strip),
-  **pocket for the ESP32** (52 x 29 mm) with four screw holes, holes for RF shield and USB connector so it sits flat. The ESP32 is 15 mm from the shaft,
-  **slot for the Hall sensor** 13 mm from the shaft,
-  **pocket for the battery** on the underside of the arm, below the LED strip side, with slots for zip ties,
- **16 ballast holes** (M3, 8 at each end of the arm), where I can screw in bolts and nuts to add weight.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/79e6d9b9b8768d468c4a81b69f6a10795cbab52ad762f9ce27fb249a4d3d320a.png)

### 5. Hall sensor and magnet

The A3144 sensor sits in the arm and a 4 mm thick magnet sits in a shallow pocket in the front plate of the bracket. I made the pocket shallow on purpose, so the magnet sticks out about 2.5 mm and the gap to the sensor is only about 2-3 mm. A3144 is not very sensitive, so a small gap is important. The magnet will be glued with hot glue, which is fine because it does not move.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/00dfcd51fbeedcde6f230358fa085475fd19207cd8a89700d336f340122349bb.png)

### 6. Balancing

The arm will spin fast, so it must be balanced. I used the rule: mass x distance from the shaft must be equal on both sides. My estimates are the LED strip about 5 g, ESP32 about 10 g, battery about 10-12 g and the boost converter about 2 g. I put the battery and the converter under the LED side, because this gives a smaller imbalance than putting them on the ESP32 side. The rest will be fixed with the ballast bolts. I will weigh the real parts in week 9.

### 7. Problems I found and fixed

- A side wall at the short end of the bracket would hit the wall screw holes, so I moved the walls to the long sides.
- The battery pocket was too close to the shaft, and the battery would touch the corners of the front plate when spinning. I moved it to 40 mm from the shaft.
- The first idea for zip tie slots made the ties cross the LED strip and cover LEDs. I changed the slots, so the ties run along the arm, next to the strip.
- I noticed that 144 LED/m strips are about 12-13 mm wide, so my first LED pocket (10.5 mm) was too narrow. I changed the pocket to 13.5mm.

### Motor speed test (0.5h)

I tested the motor with a bench power supply, an IR sensor and the ESP32, which counted the revolutions. The speed without any load was:

4 V  2500 rpm

 5 V  3250 rpm

 6 V  4100 rpm

The speed grows almost linearly with the voltage, about 800 rpm per volt, as expected for a brushed motor. For the display I only need about 1200-1800 rpm, so I will start at about 3 V. The speed will be lower with the arm attached. Lower speed also means a smaller centrifugal force on the battery and more time to send each column of the image to the LEDs.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/f7f3b8e9be1a5e8b74c0960a678634cf2c73a3028c8b5f385a7879666d7210ed.png)

### 8. Research

- **A3144 and ESP32:** the sensor works from 5 V and has an open collector output, so using the ESP32 internal pull-up to 3.3 V is safe.
- **Logic level for APA102:** the APA102 data pins should be above about 0.7 of the supply voltage, which is about 3.5 V at 5 V, and the ESP32 gives 3.3 V. It usually works, but with a small margin. First I will test it without anything extra. If the strip flickers, I will add a diode in series with the strip power supply to lower its voltage a little, and I will update the schematic.
- **LED strip price:** one AliExpress offer cost about 106PLN (26,85USD) with shipping, which is almost my whole $30 budget. I found another offer 1m 144 IP30 with a 72.79PLN (18,44USD) sale that starts tomorrow and a free delivery.I will probably need o buy this one because there is no offer with less than one meter of strip and this is the cheepest offer for 1m

### 10. README (time:0.75 h)

I rewrote the README in my GitHub repository, so that someone who has never seen the project can understand it. It now contains:

- a description of how the display works step by step, with the timing calculation
- the hardware table, the pin connections and the schematic,
- the mechanical design: the wall bracket, the arm, the Hall sensor with the magnet and the balancing,
- the motor speed test with the table of results,
- safety notes and a progress checklist.

### 11. Firmware (time: 0.25 h)

I wrote the first version of the firmware in the Arduino IDE (`firmware/spinpov/spinpov.ino` in the repo). The Hall sensor gives one pulse per revolution, and the code measures the time of the revolution. Then it turns the time since the last pulse into a column number (0-119) and sends that column to the APA102 strip over SPI. All columns are prepared in advance, so the loop only sends bytes. If the pulses stop, the LEDs switch off.

There are three test pictures: a test picture with lines at the magnet and at a quarter, a half and three quarters of a revolution (to check the direction and the offset), a rainbow that changes with the angle, and coloured rings. Settings at the top of the file (`REVERSE_DIRECTION`, `COLUMN_OFFSET`, `FLIP_ROWS`, `BRIGHTNESS`) let me correct a mirrored or shifted picture without changing the code.

The code compiles without errors for the ESP32 Dev Module. I have not tested it on hardware yet, because I do not have the LED strip and the arm is not built, so the first real test is in week 9. I wrote the first version of the code with AI (Claude), then I compiled it and read how it works.
